headline: Borrowed from
women’s medicine.
dek: Two skin treatments in this lane were studied in women. One is an estrogen.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: Studied in women
glance.line: Spironolactone’s acne trials and estriol’s skin studies enrolled only women.

glance.label: Estriol
glance.line: An estrogen. No FDA-approved estriol product exists in the US.

glance.label: Banned in sport
glance.line: Spironolactone is named under S5, diuretics and masking agents.

pull.quote: There are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol.

body: Some of the skin treatments men are offered were tested almost entirely in women. The clearest case is [[/spironolactone|spironolactone]]. FDA approved it as Aldactone in January 1960,[^aldactonefda] and its uses today are heart failure, high blood pressure and fluid build-up.[^aldactone] Acne is not one of them. Because the drug also blocks the receptor for male hormones, doctors prescribe it off-label for acne in adult women.

The two best randomized trials of spironolactone for acne enrolled only women. SAFA, in England and Wales, assigned 410 women to spironolactone or a placebo.[^safa] Its authors reported that “Spironolactone improved outcomes compared with placebo, with greater differences at week 24 than week 12.”[^safa] FASCE, in France, randomized 133 women with moderate acne to spironolactone or the antibiotic doxycycline, each with benzoyl peroxide.[^fasce] Neither trial tells us how the drug behaves in men.

The label does. It warns that “ALDACTONE can cause gynecomastia,”[^aldactone] the growth of breast tissue in men, and says that in one heart failure trial “about 9% of the male subjects developed gynecomastia.”[^aldactone] Its list of reproductive side effects includes “Decreased libido, inability to achieve or maintain erection”.[^aldactone] It can also raise potassium in the blood.[^aldactone] Athletes face a separate rule: the World Anti-Doping Agency names spironolactone among the diuretics and masking agents it bans.[^wada]

The second borrowing is a hormone. [[/estriol|Estriol]] is an estrogen, one of the female sex hormones the body makes, and it turns up in face creams. FDA is plain about it: “There are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol. Marketed drugs that contain estriol are compounded drugs, which are not FDA-approved.”[^meno] The agency adds that it “does not have evidence that drugs containing estriol are safe and effective”[^meno], or that they are safer than other estrogens.

The skin evidence for estriol comes from one group at the University of Vienna in the 1990s. A 1994 pilot study treated the faces of perimenopausal women with an estriol cream (8 patients) or an estradiol cream (10 patients) for six months.[^schmidt94] Both groups improved, and the authors judged the estriol results “slightly superior with regard to their extent and onset.”[^schmidt94] A 1996 study compared the same two creams in 59 women and reported that after six months “elasticity and firmness of the skin had markedly improved”[^schmidt96] in both groups. Neither had a placebo group, and the search found no study of estriol on men’s skin.

For contrast, several acne drugs went through FDA approval. [[/tretinoin|Tretinoin]] was approved as Retin-A in October 1971,[^retinafda] and its label says it “is indicated for topical application in the treatment of acne vulgaris.”[^retina] [[/adapalene|Adapalene]] was approved as Differin in May 1996,[^differinfda] and its 0.1% gel moved to over-the-counter sale in July 2016.[^switch] [[/benzoyl-peroxide|Benzoyl peroxide]] is sold without a prescription too, and FDA notes that some acne products containing it “have been recalled due to benzene contamination.”[^benzene] [[/clascoterone|Clascoterone]] cream was approved as Winlevi in August 2020[^winlevifda]. Its label describes it as “an androgen receptor inhibitor”[^winlevi], meaning it blocks male hormones where it is applied.

The strongest acne drug has the strictest rules. [[/isotretinoin|Isotretinoin]] was first approved as Accutane in May 1982.[^accutane] Today’s labels reserve it for “severe recalcitrant nodular acne”[^absorica] and say it is available only through a restricted program called iPLEDGE, whose goal FDA describes as “to mitigate the risk of embryo-fetal toxicity.”[^ipledge] The label also warns that it “may cause depression, psychosis and, rarely, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, suicide, and aggressive and/or violent behaviors”.[^absorica] In the UK, an expert review was set up after patients raised concerns about mental health and sexual side effects “that sometimes continue after treatment with isotretinoin has been stopped.”[^mhra]

Rosacea has its own approved drugs. [[/azelaic-acid|Azelaic acid]] gel, sold as Finacea, “is indicated for topical treatment of inflammatory papules and pustules of mild to moderate rosacea.”[^finacea] A low-dose capsule of [[/doxycycline|doxycycline]], Oracea, was approved in May 2006[^oraceafda] for “only inflammatory lesions (papules and pustules) of rosacea in adult patients.”[^oracea] [[/niacinamide|Niacinamide]], a form of vitamin B3, appears in FDA’s approval records only as one vitamin in multivitamin products, not as a skin drug.[^niacinamide]

The lane’s best-known peptide has the least behind it. [[/ghk-cu|GHK-Cu]], a copper peptide, is not FDA approved for any use. FDA lists the injected form among substances that may pose significant safety risks in compounding, warning that injected products “may pose risk for immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities.”[^cat2] Its only randomized human skin study followed patients after laser resurfacing around the mouth; 13 completed it.[^miller] Blinded evaluators found no difference between groups in redness, and while all patients improved in wrinkles and skin quality, “no differences were found between groups.”[^miller] Patients using GHK-Cu did rate their improvement higher on a questionnaire.[^miller]

One peptide in this lane is FDA approved, but for a rare disease, not for tanning. [[/afamelanotide|Afamelanotide]] was approved as Scenesse, an implant, in October 2019.[^scenessefda] Its label says it “is indicated to increase pain free light exposure in adult patients with a history of phototoxic reactions from erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP).”[^scenesse] EPP is an inherited condition in which sunlight causes severe pain in the skin. Because the drug darkens the skin, including moles and freckles, the label says that “A full body skin examination (twice yearly) is recommended”.[^scenesse] Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported.[^scenesse]

What is still not known is how most of these treatments behave in men over years. For spironolactone and estriol, the trials were run in women. For GHK-Cu, the human data come from 13 people. Compounded creams that mix these ingredients have not been tested at all in published trials, and FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA approved.[^compounding]
